In fact, the letter ‘ஹ’ was developed/ introduced just for transliteration purposes. So when there is no such letter, there can be no words either! Also, the above said use is often condemned and words beginning with ‘ha’ are often Tamilized! —Mostly in cases of proper nouns (Names). E.g.) Hindu - இந்து (Indu), Haran - அரன் (Aran), Hosur - ஓசூர் (Osur) Moreover, Tamil has its own equivalents to all the Sanskrit words and the influence of Sanskrit even sans ‘ha’ is very less.

Question: What is the most badass thing your parent has ever done?
Old_Answer: Early 2000s… Maybe 2003 or 2004. Back then, I do not think high speed broadband Internet connections existed, at least at our hometown Pondicherry. We had this age old BSNL dial-up Internet connection, connected to the landline telephone. It required us to log in with a password every time we needed to access the internet. Also, while using internet, if one was to pick up a call on the landline, internet connection would get disconnected and the log-in procedure had to be repeated. We had an internet connection at home mainly because dad had to check E-mails when not at work and clear them off before the next day. Needless to say, it was not an era of smartphones. The very concept of internet was fascinating for my sister and me! We felt thrilled being able to get information about anything with just few clicks, browse different websites and communicate through E-mails with family contacts living as far as in the USA. Contrary to Google, Yahoo’s home page itself would be awesome with multiple featured news items, links directing to Mail, Answers, Messenger, Stock market, Weather and what not! I guess it still is like that, although the traffic on the site is multifold less than Google. But what caught our eyes every time was ‘GAMES’! Yahoo used to have this concept of ‘Downloadable Games’. Only the trial version of these games could be downloaded. Full version required us to pay online in US Dollars, which was unimaginable for us. The trial version included 60 minutes of free game play, after the expiry of which only 5 minutes of gameplay would be allowed every time the game was opened. We were permitted to download only one such game every week or every 10 days, as the internet bills were also relatively expensive those days. We were allowed to access the internet only when our father was at home. We didn’t have a choice either, because only he knew the password. Question: As an Indian, what's your favourite thing about India?
Old_Answer: Food! I’m a strong believer of ‘Be a Roman when in Rome’. While travelling or moving out of India to another country, adapting to changes might prove to be a difficult task. But, in the long run, that is what will help one express themself and interact better, with the local population. Be it language, lifestyle or culture, adapting to the new place offers its own advantages! This can also be applied to regional differences within India. But, one exception is FOOD! Nothing beats Indian food. No wonder millions of Non-Resident Indians/ Persons of Indian Origin prefer and have Indian food, regardless of how long they’ve been away from home. No amount of westernisation has killed the charm and heritage of Indian cuisines. (Pictures from Google Images) It’s not that I always have Indian food wherever I go. I do explore new places, new restaurants and cuisines abroad; all of that probably for a maximum of couple of days. The Indian in me would then crave for the authentic, spicy, aromatic Indian food! Finding an Indian restaurant in an unknown land is like a child lost in a carnival, finally finding its parents! Though I’m a South Indian, I like South Indian and North Indian cuisines alike. Being in a different country is when, we realize, being an Indian is more important than finding differences within us based on region, language etc. @ Khana Khazana Indian restaurant, Kigali (Rwanda) Now, Rwanda is an East-African country where there isn’t even a reasonable expatriate Indian population. Question: What is your salary? Are you happy with it?
Old_Answer: I’m a doctor and I’m paid ₹5,000 per month. Obviously, I’m not happy with it. I’m currently a Compulsory Rotatory Residential Intern (CRRI) doctor/ House Surgeon at the Government Medical College - Hospital of Pondicherry. We started our internship on February 19th, 2020. A month later, COVID-19 was in the news and soon our hospital became the state’s COVID designated hospital and all other services were shut. Today, with 13500+ total cases and 211 deaths, Pondicherry tops the country in the number of positive COVID-19 cases per million! Ever since there were interns in our hospital (from 2015), this amount of ₹5000 has been the standard monthly stipend. No payslip, no Government Order, no whatsoever. It comes to ₹161/ day which is far less than most daily wage labourers in the country. Even worse, the stipend is not credited to our bank accounts every month. It is usually credited at the end of three months as ₹15,000. This stipend amount is the least of all Government Medical Colleges in the country. Funny fact is that ours is allegedly the country’s most expensive Government Medical College, tuition-fee wise. It used to be ₹70,000/year when I was a UG student. Now, I understand it is 1 lakh+ per year, from my juniors. Multiple attempts in representing this issue to the government, including indefinite student strikes, RTI complaints etc. yielded nothing. Whilst this stipend amount is not acceptable even during normal times, imagine working day and night during a pandemic period for ₹161/ day. Our valuable training period is also lost in the name of COVID-19. We have completely lost hope on the government regarding stipend hike. Therefore, we have not resorted to any more strikes. We have been posted in all areas of the COVID hospital including COVID wards, COVID ICU and casualty. While this unhappy and unrewarded feeling will definitely continue to prevail, I’m sure this has, not in anyway, affected the healthcare we provide to our patients, nor will it in the future. This holds good, COVID or not :) (Picture from my phone gallery)

But whatever I have mentioned above, are becoming more and more common. Fortunately, we can prevent or diagnose them at a very early stage. Let us or our dear ones not succumb to them!
